assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, make it possible to interrogate thousands of atoms at once with the Doppler and recoil shifts removed, and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is precision atomic physics of the kind I know well. It redefines what can be measured and opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic time dilation over millimetres, and searches for new physics. The central idea is simple and clear, and the result is large.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group pushed the systematic accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 level and carried out the gravitational redshift tests. Two laureates give a clean and fair configuration. Other groups, such as Lemke/Ludlow at NIST and the PTB and Paris groups, made important contributions, but the supplied credit supports these two.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories have reproduced and compared lattice clocks, with agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level. The field is mature and robust, and recognition is timely. The Nobel Prize in 2005 (Hall and Hänsch for the comb) and in 2012 (Wineland, with Haroche) already covered adjacent technology, so the committee must be clear about what is new here.
uncertainties: How the committee weighs a metrology achievement against a discovery, given that the prize is described as a major tool rather than a new phenomenon.
Whether the ion-clock and comb lineage (Wineland, Hall, Hänsch) leaves enough room for the lattice-clock contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases with tunable interactions turned the BEC-BCS crossover into a laboratory system. The result is fundamental: a controlled bridge between molecular condensates and BCS-like superfluidity, with universal behaviour at unitarity that connects to neutron stars and the physics of superconductors. It was in part unexpected, and it gave quantitative tests of many-body theory.
assessment.attribution: Grimm's group produced the molecular BEC and its crossover into the fermionic regime. Salomon's group measured the equation of state and collective modes. Thomas's group realised the strongly interacting degenerate gas and showed the signature of its universal behaviour. Several other groups contributed at the same time (Jin, Ketterle, Zwierlein), so the allocation of credit is delicate, and the late Deborah Jin cannot be recognised.
assessment.maturity: The results have been reproduced by many independent laboratories and verified against theory and Monte Carlo calculations. The field is mature, so recognition would be late rather than premature.
uncertainties: The credit for the first observation of the condensate of fermion pairs is split among several teams, and the proposed three-person set omits other major contributors.
A prize for ultracold gases already exists (2001, 1997), so the novelty relative to those has to be argued.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters. The Mott insulator transition and then fermionic Hubbard physics, with single-site resolution, made it possible to simulate strongly correlated matter in a way that is understandable in terms of simple images. The impact on many-body physics is deep and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and coworkers) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition, and Bloch and Esslinger have led the development of the fermionic and the high-resolution direction. Five names are credited and only three can be selected. I choose a combination of theory and the two experimental leaders, but Greiner and Cirac have strong claims, so the allocation is open.
assessment.maturity: Experimental results are reproduced across many laboratories, and the quantum gas microscope is established. The quantum simulation programme is still developing, and the ultimate value (answers to open questions such as the fermionic Hubbard phase diagram) is not yet in hand, so there is some risk that recognition is early.
uncertainties: Whether the main discovery is the Mott transition, the platform or a later physical result about the Hubbard model.
The Zoller overlap with trapped ions and Rydberg arrays complicates the choice of laureates across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation at high fidelity show control over single quantum systems in a way I find convincing. It is a foundation for quantum information processing, and trapped-ion platforms are among the best quantum computers and simulators now existing.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller gave the proposal and Blatt (together with Wineland's group, who were already recognised in 2012) built the experimental implementations of gates, entanglement and algorithms. Combination of theory and experiment is natural, but Zoller may be favoured elsewhere in the list, and Wineland's earlier prize overlaps with the experimental claim.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in several laboratories, with the proposal now more than thirty years old. The platform is mature, though the larger question of scalable quantum computing is still open.
uncertainties: How much of the experimental credit has already been recognised by the 2012 prize.
Whether trapped-ion computing counts as a discovery or an engineering route.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state, and then entangling and squeezing them, speaks directly to the question of where the quantum world meets the classical one. This is the kind of discovery I find most interesting, and it matches the 2025 prize theme of macroscopic quantum behaviour.
assessment.attribution: Cleland's group reached the ground state of a mechanical resonator coupled to a qubit, Kippenberg's and Painter's groups cooled optical resonators into the quantum regime, and Aspelmeyer's group did quantum optomechanics experiments and entanglement. Four names are credited; I can only select three, and omitting Painter is a real difficulty because the credit is shared.
assessment.maturity: Several independent laboratories have shown quantum control. The field is fast-moving, and the strongest results (entanglement, squeezing, tests of macroscopic superposition) are still growing, so some of it may be premature.
uncertainties: The distribution of credit between the ground-state cooling milestone and the larger programme.
Whether a prize in 2025 for macroscopic quantum effects makes a second prize close to that theme too early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of single Rydberg atoms, with tweezers and strong dipole blockade interaction, produce controllable many-body quantum states and gates. The work has led to simulations of quantum magnets and exotic phases, and a route to quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Lukin's group (with Greiner and others) demonstrated the large programmable arrays, Browaeys's group and Grangier's group demonstrated blockade and individual-atom control, and Saffman proposed and demonstrated gates. Five names are credited. Zoller and Grangier also have significant claims, and a fair three-person set is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories have reproduced it, but most of the results are less than ten years old and the key physics claims (such as spin liquids and scalable error-corrected computing) are still evolving. Recognition now would likely be early.
uncertainties: Whether the fundamental discovery is the blockade, the tweezer array platform or the use of the arrays for simulation.
Early maturity relative to older AMO candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics brings strong coupling between an artificial atom and a single photon on a chip, and it is the basis of superconducting quantum computers. The idea is conceptually elegant and has led to a great deal of physics, including dispersive readout and photon-number resolution.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 theory proposal and the Yale experiment; Wallraff led the first strong-coupling demonstration. Four names are credited. I would pick the three in the original proposal and demonstration, but this choice leaves out Blais, whose role in the theory was decisive.
assessment.maturity: The effect is reproduced and the technology is mature. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits has already honoured part of the same community, so the timing and overlap are open questions.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize for superconducting circuit macroscopic quantum effects.
Whether the main significance is a fundamental discovery or an enabling technology for quantum computation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that phases in quantum mechanics have physical, topological content. This is fundamental and unexpected, and it influences atomic physics, molecular physics, condensed matter and optics.
assessment.attribution: Berry's 1984 paper is the clear source of the geometric phase, and Aharonov and Bohm gave the 1959 effect. Bohm is deceased, and Aharonov and Casher and others (Pancharatnam, Simon, Wilczek and Zee) played roles, so a clean configuration is not guaranteed, although the supplied two-name credit is possible.
assessment.maturity: The concepts are thoroughly confirmed and have been used for decades, but the time since the original work is long, and the committee may find it hard to define one decisive discovery that has not already been honoured through its consequences.
uncertainties: The credit for the geometric phase is spread across several earlier works, and the Aharonov-Bohm co-originator cannot be honoured.
Whether the committee sees this as one discovery or as two distinct contributions.
